entries.title: I Corinthians 11:1
segments: In all things.  'All' is often used in the New Testament in a general sense, not necessarily including every one (
).  Here the apostle himself mentions some exceptions, but thoughtfully begins by commending their faithfulness on the whole or for the most part.

entries.title: I Corinthians 11:2
segments: Traditions. Matters orally delivered; ordinarily meaning handed down from generation to generation; but here referring to the precepts of doctrine or duty orally delivered by the apostles to the churches in the first Christian generation.

entries.title: I Corinthians 11:3
segments: The head of every man is Christ.  There are two Greek words for 'man'; one for man as a human being; the other contrasting man with woman or child; the latter form is used for man in every instance in this chapter (

). Christ is normally and rightly the head of every man, actually of every Christian.
 

 
 The head of the woman is the man.  More fully explained in
The head of Christ is God.  Said of Christ in his mediatorial capacity (

entries.title: I Corinthians 11:4
segments:
:16
 
 Every man praying or prophesying, etc.  The propriety of covering or veiling the head is one to be understood in accordance with the customs of those countries at that period.  The veil in public places was then and there the mark of honorable and modest womanhood, and hence not to be disregarded by the Christian woman.  Other times and lands have other forms of expressing deference and modesty.  Any defiance of custom, which would indicate the lack of these qualities, would be censurable still.
 

 
 Every woman praying or prophesying. This, in connection with (

entries.title: I Corinthians 11:11
segments: In the Lord.  The spiritual unity of man and wife, in spite of differences of social relations and requirements, is meant (

entries.title: I Corinthians 11:20
segments:
:22
 
 When therefore ye assemble, etc.  Disorders at the Lord's supper may have arisen from connecting it with the 'love-feasts' of the early church.  See notes on

.
 

 
 Have ye not houses to eat and to drink in?  The fault was in making the sacrament a supper, a mere ordinary meal.  The rudeness and selfishness displayed were disgraceful incidents.

entries.title: I Corinthians 11:23
segments:
:25
 
 For I received of the Lord, etc.  This is the fourth account of the institution of the Lord's supper; the other three are in
Mk 14.22-24; Lu 22.17-20.  The repetition in all four instances of the words of institution make them the most absolutely certain of all the utterances of our Lord.

entries.title: I Corinthians 11:27
segments: Guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.  'Of' has here the sense of 'in respect to'; guilty of profaning the elements used in the communion of which the Lord had said: 'This is my body; this is my blood.'

entries.title: I Corinthians 11:30
segments: Many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep.  Numerous commentators regard the illness as physical, and the sleep as the sleep of death; both sent as divine judgment.  Others hold that spiritual weakness and sickness and apathy or deadness (sleep) of soul are indicated.
